sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Toilet training struggles happen when children choose not to use the toilet. It's important to remember that children can succeed at using the toilet but in their own time. ... Choose the words your family will use to describe body parts, urine, and bowel movements. Avoid words that are negative, like dirty, naughty, or stinky. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. Books or toys for "potty time" may help make this time more fun. ... Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... When your children feel the urge to poop, you might notice grunting, squatting, or freezing. ... Explain briefly to your children that these signs mean a poop is about to come. If your children tell you about a wet diaper, praise them for "using their words." ... Talk with them about how they will now be in charge of their pee and poop. Read children's books about using the toilet to help the process make sense and seem inviting and exciting. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Gently help them overcome their hesitation. Then help them stay in charge by having them be in charge of the cleanup.
sources.supports: Potty training advice from the AAP: children learn in their own time, positive words, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, books, a role model, signs of a poop coming, being in charge, a morning routine, hesitation and cleanup. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: When toilet training starts, switch to big-kid underwear. ... Be precise with praise. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... Try to stay calm about toilet training. Remember that children control when and where they pee and poop. So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... Understand their fear. Some children believe that their pee and poop are part of their bodies. They may be scared the toilet will flush parts of them away. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... Toilet training is a learning experience.
sources.supports: Big-kid underwear, specific praise without treats, avoiding power struggles, staying calm, fear of the flush and letting the child flush. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: When toilet training starts, switch to big-kid underwear. ... Be precise with praise. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... Try to stay calm about toilet training. Remember that children control when and where they pee and poop. So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... Understand their fear. Some children believe that their pee and poop are part of their bodies. They may be scared the toilet will flush parts of them away. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... Toilet training is a learning experience.
sources.supports: Big-kid underwear, specific praise without treats, avoiding power struggles, staying calm, fear of the flush and letting the child flush. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Toilet training struggles happen when children choose not to use the toilet. It's important to remember that children can succeed at using the toilet but in their own time. ... Choose the words your family will use to describe body parts, urine, and bowel movements. Avoid words that are negative, like dirty, naughty, or stinky. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. Books or toys for "potty time" may help make this time more fun. ... Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... When your children feel the urge to poop, you might notice grunting, squatting, or freezing. ... Explain briefly to your children that these signs mean a poop is about to come. If your children tell you about a wet diaper, praise them for "using their words." ... Talk with them about how they will now be in charge of their pee and poop. Read children's books about using the toilet to help the process make sense and seem inviting and exciting. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Gently help them overcome their hesitation. Then help them stay in charge by having them be in charge of the cleanup.
sources.supports: Potty training advice from the AAP: children learn in their own time, positive words, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, books, a role model, signs of a poop coming, being in charge, a morning routine, hesitation and cleanup. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.quote: When toilet training starts, switch to big-kid underwear. ... Be precise with praise. ... Avoid treats and punishments. ... When your children succeed, be specific about why you are proud. ... Avoid a power struggle. ... Try to stay calm about toilet training. Remember that children control when and where they pee and poop. So power struggles, begging, pleading, rewarding, and punishing keep children from managing their own toileting. ... Understand their fear. Some children believe that their pee and poop are part of their bodies. They may be scared the toilet will flush parts of them away. ... To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet. ... Toilet training is a learning experience.
sources.supports: Big-kid underwear, specific praise without treats, avoiding power struggles, staying calm, fear of the flush and letting the child flush. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: The Right Age to Potty Train
sources.quote: Toilet training struggles happen when children choose not to use the toilet. It's important to remember that children can succeed at using the toilet but in their own time. ... Choose the words your family will use to describe body parts, urine, and bowel movements. Avoid words that are negative, like dirty, naughty, or stinky. ... Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. Books or toys for "potty time" may help make this time more fun. ... Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. ... When your children feel the urge to poop, you might notice grunting, squatting, or freezing. ... Explain briefly to your children that these signs mean a poop is about to come. If your children tell you about a wet diaper, praise them for "using their words." ... Talk with them about how they will now be in charge of their pee and poop. Read children's books about using the toilet to help the process make sense and seem inviting and exciting. ... Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. ... Gently help them overcome their hesitation. Then help them stay in charge by having them be in charge of the cleanup.
sources.supports: Potty training advice from the AAP: children learn in their own time, positive words, a potty chair where the feet reach the floor, books, a role model, signs of a poop coming, being in charge, a morning routine, hesitation and cleanup. An American page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Experts weigh in: How can I get my young child less anxious about starting school?
sources.publisher: Understood (experts including Janine Domingues, Child Mind Institute)
sources.quote: Most young children are creatures of habit and thrive on routines and schedules. ... Your child may have a stomachache, usually in the morning before school or in the evening before going to bed. ... Explore back-to-school book lists for preschoolers and grade-schoolers.
sources.supports: Young children thrive on routines, a stomachache before school is a common physical sign, and back-to-school books are a suggested tool.

sources.title: Back to School
sources.quote: It's also important to talk to kids about any worries and offer support. ... Eat a healthy breakfast. They're more alert and do better in school if they eat a good breakfast every day. ... Organize and set out what they need the night before. Homework and books should be put in their backpacks by the door and clothes should be laid out in their bedrooms. ... But a few kids develop real physical symptoms, such as headaches or stomachaches, at the start of school.
sources.supports: Talking about worries, breakfast, setting out backpack and clothes the night before, and that a few kids get stomachaches at the start of school.

sources.title: 8 ways to make school morning routines easier
sources.quote: Ask your child to pick out an outfit for the next day. ... Check that all books, homework, and changes of clothing are packed up and by the door. ... If you have breakfast as a family, set the breakfast table. ... Wake up a little earlier than your child. ... Try not to be racing around to get yourself ready at the same time. This will lower the stress level for both of you. ... Set your child's alarm to play a favorite song. Try waking your child up with lots of snuggles or a favorite breakfast. ... Make every day as predictable as you can. Follow the same routine before and after school. ... Wake up, wash face, eat breakfast, get dressed, brush teeth, go over the day's schedule, leave for school. A picture schedule can be extra helpful for kids who struggle with reading. ... Designate spots for school supplies, sports gear, coats, and jackets. ... Make sure there are clocks "in your face" around the house. ... Give manageable countdowns, like "At 7:25, it'll be time to put your shoes on." ... Have your child check and re-check to make sure everything's packed before leaving the house. Younger kids can come up with a silly phrase or song to help remember all the books and materials they need each morning. ... if your child gets ready for school and still has time to spare before it's time to leave, play a quick game together or read a book.
sources.supports: Night-before preparation, a predictable routine, designated spots, clocks and countdowns, a double-check, a gentle wake-up, the adult starting early and a game if time is left. An American page that also covers neurodivergent kids, used as general advice.

sources.title: Sleep and Your School-Aged Child
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: School-age kids need 9–12 hours of sleep a night. ... Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime. ... Set regular bedtimes and wake-up times. To be sure your child gets enough sleep, decide when your child needs to get up for school in the morning and count back 9–12 hours from there. On weekends, try to stick to the sleep schedule as close as you can. Aim for sleep or wake-up times no more than an hour later than on weekdays.
sources.supports: Sleep needs of school-age children, screens off an hour before bed, counting back from the wake-up time and keeping weekend times close to weekdays.

sources.title: 8 ways to make school morning routines easier
sources.quote: Ask your child to pick out an outfit for the next day. ... Check that all books, homework, and changes of clothing are packed up and by the door. ... If you have breakfast as a family, set the breakfast table. ... Wake up a little earlier than your child. ... Try not to be racing around to get yourself ready at the same time. This will lower the stress level for both of you. ... Set your child's alarm to play a favorite song. Try waking your child up with lots of snuggles or a favorite breakfast. ... Make every day as predictable as you can. Follow the same routine before and after school. ... Wake up, wash face, eat breakfast, get dressed, brush teeth, go over the day's schedule, leave for school. A picture schedule can be extra helpful for kids who struggle with reading. ... Designate spots for school supplies, sports gear, coats, and jackets. ... Make sure there are clocks "in your face" around the house. ... Give manageable countdowns, like "At 7:25, it'll be time to put your shoes on." ... Have your child check and re-check to make sure everything's packed before leaving the house. Younger kids can come up with a silly phrase or song to help remember all the books and materials they need each morning. ... if your child gets ready for school and still has time to spare before it's time to leave, play a quick game together or read a book.
sources.supports: Night-before preparation, a predictable routine, designated spots, clocks and countdowns, a double-check, a gentle wake-up, the adult starting early and a game if time is left. An American page that also covers neurodivergent kids, used as general advice.

sources.title: Experts weigh in: How can I get my young child less anxious about starting school?
sources.publisher: Understood (experts including Janine Domingues, Child Mind Institute)
sources.quote: Most young children are creatures of habit and thrive on routines and schedules. ... Your child may have a stomachache, usually in the morning before school or in the evening before going to bed. ... Explore back-to-school book lists for preschoolers and grade-schoolers.
sources.supports: Young children thrive on routines, a stomachache before school is a common physical sign, and back-to-school books are a suggested tool.

sources.title: Back to School
sources.quote: It's also important to talk to kids about any worries and offer support. ... Eat a healthy breakfast. They're more alert and do better in school if they eat a good breakfast every day. ... Organize and set out what they need the night before. Homework and books should be put in their backpacks by the door and clothes should be laid out in their bedrooms. ... But a few kids develop real physical symptoms, such as headaches or stomachaches, at the start of school.
sources.supports: Talking about worries, breakfast, setting out backpack and clothes the night before, and that a few kids get stomachaches at the start of school.

sources.title: Sleep and Your School-Aged Child
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD, January 2021)
sources.quote: School-age kids need 9–12 hours of sleep a night. ... Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime. ... Set regular bedtimes and wake-up times. To be sure your child gets enough sleep, decide when your child needs to get up for school in the morning and count back 9–12 hours from there. On weekends, try to stick to the sleep schedule as close as you can. Aim for sleep or wake-up times no more than an hour later than on weekdays.
sources.supports: Sleep needs of school-age children, screens off an hour before bed, counting back from the wake-up time and keeping weekend times close to weekdays.

sources.title: 8 ways to make school morning routines easier
sources.quote: Ask your child to pick out an outfit for the next day. ... Check that all books, homework, and changes of clothing are packed up and by the door. ... If you have breakfast as a family, set the breakfast table. ... Wake up a little earlier than your child. ... Try not to be racing around to get yourself ready at the same time. This will lower the stress level for both of you. ... Set your child's alarm to play a favorite song. Try waking your child up with lots of snuggles or a favorite breakfast. ... Make every day as predictable as you can. Follow the same routine before and after school. ... Wake up, wash face, eat breakfast, get dressed, brush teeth, go over the day's schedule, leave for school. A picture schedule can be extra helpful for kids who struggle with reading. ... Designate spots for school supplies, sports gear, coats, and jackets. ... Make sure there are clocks "in your face" around the house. ... Give manageable countdowns, like "At 7:25, it'll be time to put your shoes on." ... Have your child check and re-check to make sure everything's packed before leaving the house. Younger kids can come up with a silly phrase or song to help remember all the books and materials they need each morning. ... if your child gets ready for school and still has time to spare before it's time to leave, play a quick game together or read a book.
sources.supports: Night-before preparation, a predictable routine, designated spots, clocks and countdowns, a double-check, a gentle wake-up, the adult starting early and a game if time is left. An American page that also covers neurodivergent kids, used as general advice.
